Monsoon 2018

Thin walls, strong curves

How a row of ferrocement arches, only a few centimetres thick, now holds a river pond in Sakri Taluka, Dhule.

Jitendra Sonawane · Agriculture Engineer

Check dams in rural watershed work are usually heavy: masonry, gabions or thick concrete walls. They work, but they need a lot of material and a big budget. So we asked a simple question: what if the dam relied on shape instead of weight? The answer was an arch-type ferrocement check dam, built with support from the Deshbandhu and Manju Gupta Foundation and technical guidance from Dr. Diwekar. As far as we know, it is one of the first check dams of this kind in India.

Let the arch do the work

An arch carries load along its curve instead of bending under it. When water presses on the curved upstream face, the whole arch goes into compression, and cement mortar is very strong in compression.

That is why a curved shell 50–75 mm thick can hold back water that would need a far thicker straight wall. Our dam is a row of semicircular ferrocement shells, each about 2 m across and 3 m high, standing on a PCC foundation keyed into rock, with solid abutments on both banks.

How we built it

Foundation

Excavated down to hard rock; cast a PCC base and cut-off so water cannot slip under the dam.

Skeleton

Bent 8 mm TMT bars into hoops and verticals to form each arch.

Mesh

Wrapped one layer of weld mesh and two layers of chicken mesh around the skeleton.

Mortar

Pressed rich 1:2 cement mortar through the mesh from both faces, then cured it well.

Most of the work used local labour. There was no heavy machinery and no large formwork, only careful tying and plastering by village masons.

The result

In the monsoon of 2018 the dam filled and overflowed exactly as designed. Water spilled over each arch crest in a smooth curtain, and the pond behind it stretched well upstream.

Watch the dam in actionyoutu.be/O-X__9Lqt7g

The arch was never the hard part. The foundation it stands on is.

Why this matters

Less material

A thin shell uses far less cement and stone than a gravity wall of the same height.

Local skills

Masons and villagers learn mesh tying and plastering quickly.

Replicable

One arch is the unit; repeat it to fit any nala width.

What we learned

A thin arch is strong, but the rest of the structure must be designed with the same care. The foundation, the buttresses between the arches and the anchorage into rock carry everything the arches pass on. The dam also has to resist uplift and sliding at its base, not only water pressure on its face.

Taking those lessons forward, I have built a design and estimate tool for this type of dam. It covers hydraulic design, arch and shell checks, stability with all the forces acting, linked drawings and a complete bill of quantities, so anyone planning one can start from a sound, checked design.

Thank you

To the Deshbandhu and Manju Gupta Foundation for believing in an untested idea, to Dr. Diwekar for his guidance, and to the villagers and masons whose hands built it. If you work in watershed development, soil and water conservation or rural infrastructure and want to try this design, message me. I am happy to share what we learned.
